newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban hold pass despite fresh assault.
newsitem.headline: Taleban hold pass despite fresh assault.

text.p: Taleban troops maintained their grip on two strategic passes north of the Afghan capital on Thursday despite a third blistering assault by forces loyal to the ousted Afghan government.

Fierce heavy artillery and rocket duels churned up columns of dust around the De Sabz pass, 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul, with shells and rockets pounding the barren mountainside several times a minute.
But despite their third attack in nine days on De Sabz and a second pass, Khair Khana, the former Afghan government's forces appeared no closer to seizing the strategic heights above Kabul.

"On the roads on both fronts, the lines have not changed very much," Mehrabuddin Masstan, a spokesman for the commander of former government forces, Ahmad Shah Masood, told reporters in the town of Jabal os-Siraj to the north.
"Especially on the new road (De Sabz pass), there was an immense amount of shelling but not much progress," Masstan said.
The assault, which began at around 6 a.m. (0130 GMT) on Thursday, petered out in the early afternoon, with both sides shelling intermittently.
It was the third assault by the anti-Taleban alliance, made up of Masood's troops and heavy weapons together with those of the northern Uzbek leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The passes are prized by the former government as "the gates to Kabul".
A senior source in Masood's camp said retaking Kabul from the radical Islamic Taleban militia, which seized the city at the end of September, was politically as well as militarily vital.
"We must take Kabul as this will be a sign that we are serious and other provinces will follow (revolt against the Taleban)," the source said.
"We got to a few hundred metres (yards) from the road but there are still Taleban tanks on the pass," said Amir Mohammad, a commander with Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction.
He spoke at a command post next to a mud observation tower behind the front line on the De Sabz pass, where he was resting after the morning's inferno, a red cotton scarf wrapped around his neck.
"We've stopped for lunch," joked Amir Mohammad as the fighting died down.
The anti-Taleban alliance's troops and armour hold perilously exposed positions on the empty hills below the pass.
Former government commanders said fighting also raged around the village of Hussein Kot, about 20 km (12 miles) north of Kabul.
Shells slammed into the fields beside the road to the village.
But fighting failed to disrupt a busy market day in the village of Qarabagh, around 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul.
Asked if he was concerned by the fighting around him, 40-year-old Allamir (one name), wearing a white turban and stomping home with a bag of tea, replied: "Only Allah knows my future."
